title: What does the Rail Safety National Law require for rail safety worker competence?
description: Section 117 of the Rail Safety National Law, AQF based competence assessment, regulation 30 competence records and what ONRSR expects in a rail SMS.
shortAnswer: Section 117 of the Rail Safety National Law requires every accredited rail transport operator in Australia to ensure each rail safety worker has the competence to carry out their rail safety work. Competence must be assessed against Australian Qualifications Framework units where they apply, and by reference to the knowledge and skills needed to work safely. Operators must keep competence records under regulation 30 of the National Regulations, and the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator expects periodic reassessment.
keyTakeaways: Section 117(1) of the Rail Safety National Law (RSNL) makes the rail transport operator responsible for each rail safety worker's competence, with a maximum penalty of $500,000 for a body corporate.

Competence must be assessed against applicable Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF) qualifications and units, or prescribed competencies, and by reference to the knowledge and skills to work safely (s117(2)); an alternative is allowed only where AQF assessment is not reasonably practicable and the Regulator is satisfied (s117(4)).

Regulation 30 of the Rail Safety National Law National Regulations 2012 lists what competence records must contain, including training duration, units attained, reassessment and retraining dates, and the assessor's name and qualifications.
Section 118 requires each rail safety worker to carry identification that lets a rail safety officer check their type of competence and training.
ONRSR's Safety Management System Guideline (version 2.2, March 2, 2026) expects risk-based competence management and periodic reassessment of rail safety workers.
jurisdiction: Australia (jurisdictions applying the Rail Safety National Law)
regulator: Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator (ONRSR)
appliesTo: Accredited rail transport operators: rail infrastructure managers and rolling stock operators, including tourist and heritage operators
Rail safety workers, including drivers, train controllers, signallers, shunters, maintainers, track workers and safe working system developers
Contractors and labor hire providers whose workers carry out rail safety work on an operator's network or rolling stock
Training and assessment providers delivering rail qualifications and units of competence

sections.heading: What does section 117 of the Rail Safety National Law require?

blocks.text: Section 117 places a direct duty on the rail transport operator to make sure each rail safety worker is competent for the rail safety work they do. In the [Rail Safety National Law](https://www.legislation.sa.gov.au/_legislation-documents/lz/c/a/rail-safety-national-law-south-australia-act-2012/current/2012.14.auth.pdf), which is set out in the Schedule to the Rail Safety National Law (South Australia) Act 2012 and applied by other participating jurisdictions, subsection (1) reads:

blocks.title: RSNL section 117(1)
blocks.text: "A rail transport operator must ensure that each rail safety worker who is to carry out rail safety work in relation to railway operations in respect of which the operator is required to be accredited has the competence to carry out that work." Maximum penalty: $50,000 for an individual and $500,000 for a body corporate.
The section then sets how competence is assessed, what counts as evidence, when an alternative is allowed, and record keeping:

items: **Assessment basis (s117(2)):** competence must be assessed in accordance with any AQF qualification and units of competence applicable to the work, or if none apply, any prescribed qualifications or competencies, and by reference to the knowledge and skills that would enable the worker to carry out the work safely.
**Evidence (s117(3)):** an AQF certificate is evidence that the worker holds those qualifications or units.

**Alternative pathway (s117(4)):** where AQF based assessment is not reasonably practicable, the operator must satisfy the Regulator that the worker has otherwise acquired the necessary qualifications and competencies and has the knowledge and skills to work safely.
**Further training (s117(5)):** nothing stops an operator requiring more training before work starts.
**Records (s117(6)):** records must be kept in accordance with the national regulations, with a maximum penalty of $50,000 for a body corporate.
**False information (s117(6a)):** giving false or misleading information in a competence assessment is an offense with a maximum penalty of $10,000.

sections.heading: Who counts as a rail safety worker?

blocks.text: Anyone who carries out rail safety work as defined in section 8 of the RSNL, which is much broader than train crew. The definition covers driving or despatching rolling stock, signalling and communications that can affect train movements, coupling and uncoupling, and constructing, maintaining, inspecting or testing rolling stock or rail infrastructure.

It also covers work that places a person at risk of exposure to moving rolling stock, installing or maintaining rail telecommunications and traction power, certifying the safety of infrastructure or rolling stock, decommissioning, developing or monitoring safe working systems, and managing or monitoring passenger safety. ONRSR's guideline gives examples such as train controllers, shunters, signal fitters, engineers who certify assets, and train control planners.

Because the definition is activity based, a [training needs analysis](/guides/how-to-conduct-a-training-needs-analysis) should start from tasks, not job titles. An engineer who signs off a track possession plan may be a rail safety worker even if they never go near the track.

sections.heading: What competence records must a rail transport operator keep?

blocks.text: Regulation 30 of the [Rail Safety National Law National Regulations 2012](https://www.legislation.sa.gov.au/_legislation-documents/lz/c/r/rail-safety-national-law-national-regulations-2012/current/2012.255.auth.pdf) prescribes the content. For the purposes of s117(6), records must include details of:

items: The rail safety training undertaken by each worker, including when it was undertaken and its duration.

The worker's qualifications and competencies, including where applicable the units of competence attained, the level of qualification, if and when a reassessment of competence is to be conducted, if and when retraining is due, and the date any retraining is undertaken.
The name of the organization that conducted the training or retraining.
The name and qualifications of the person who assessed the worker's competence.

blocks.text: Clause 24 of Schedule 1 to the same Regulations also requires the operator's safety management system to contain "procedures and, where necessary, standards to ensure compliance with section 117". Section 118 of the RSNL adds that each rail safety worker must have identification sufficient for a rail safety officer to check the type of competence and training the worker holds, and must produce it on request.

blocks.title: Reassessment dates are part of the record
blocks.text: Regulation 30 does not set a reassessment interval, but it does require the record to show if and when reassessment and retraining are due. An operator that cannot show a planned reassessment date for a worker has a records gap, not just a scheduling gap.

sections.heading: What does ONRSR expect to see in a competence management system?

blocks.text: ONRSR expects risk-based competence management that identifies required competencies, trains and assesses against the AQF or an equivalent, keeps records, allows qualifications to be checked and reassesses workers periodically. These expectations are set out in section 6.24 of ONRSR's [Safety Management System Guideline](https://www.onrsr.com.au/documents/Guideline/SMS-Guideline.pdf), version 2.2, approved on March 2, 2026.

Under the heading "As a minimum ONRSR expects", the guideline says operators must have processes and procedures to demonstrate that rail safety workers have the knowledge and skills to work safely, have been trained in accordance with the AQTF and AQF or equivalent, that records of training have been retained, that qualifications can be checked, and that "there is a periodic reassessment of rail safety workers". It lists five implementation steps: identify the required competencies of the work, assess training and qualification options, establish a competency training and assessment implementation plan, source accredited assessors, and undertake training and assessment.

On the alternative pathway, the guideline gives examples of why AQF assessment may not be reasonably practicable: no available registered training organization, prohibitive cost, geographic distance and a small workforce. Alternative assessment procedures must be fully documented. For in-house "enterprise attainment" programs, the documentation should note that the qualification is not recognized under the AQF and is not transferable outside the organization.

sections.heading: How can operators map RSNL competence obligations to evidence?

blocks.text: ONRSR rail safety officers check competence against the Law, the Regulations and the guideline together. Combining all three sources, the summary below pairs each duty with its owner, its timing and the record that demonstrates it.

blocks.text: For the reassessment interval, operators commonly combine risk, task frequency and incident data, as described in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles). Practical assessment design is covered in [how to set up verification of competency](/guides/how-to-set-up-verification-of-competency).

sections.heading: How does competence relate to other RSNL worker programs, and is the law changing?

blocks.text: Competence is one of several worker obligations in the same Division of the RSNL. Sections 114, 115 and 116 require accredited operators to implement a health and fitness program, a drug and alcohol management program and a fatigue risk management program for rail safety workers, each with a maximum penalty of $500,000 for a body corporate. ONRSR notes that the current edition of the National Standard for Health Assessment of Rail Safety Workers took effect on November 11, 2024.

The RSNL is under reform. According to ONRSR's [RSNL review page](https://www.onrsr.com.au/industry-information/rail-safety-national-law-review), Infrastructure and Transport Ministers supported 24 recommendations from the National Transport Commission's review in 2024, including 12 legislative reforms being progressed by the NTC. As at November 2026, section 117 and regulation 30 remain as quoted on this page; operators should track the NTC's legislative work and update their procedures using [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each class of rail safety work in section 8 to the AQF units and operator specific knowledge it requires, then defines assessment points and reassessment triggers before any training is written. The resulting structure produces the regulation 30 record fields directly, so an operator can show which competence each worker holds, how it was assessed and when it is next due.

faqs.q: Does section 117 set a fixed reassessment period for rail safety workers?
faqs.a: No. Neither section 117 nor regulation 30 sets a fixed interval. Regulation 30 requires records to show if and when reassessment and retraining are due, and ONRSR's guideline expects periodic reassessment managed on a risk basis, so each operator sets and justifies its own intervals.

faqs.q: Can an operator rely on in-house training instead of AQF units?
faqs.a: Only where AQF based assessment is not reasonably practicable and the operator satisfies ONRSR that the worker has the necessary competencies and the knowledge and skills to work safely. ONRSR expects the alternative method to be fully documented, and in-house qualifications are not recognized under the AQF or transferable.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for a contractor's competence?
faqs.a: Section 117 places the duty on the rail transport operator for each rail safety worker who carries out rail safety work in its accredited operations, which includes contractors. Operators typically require contractors to supply competence records in the regulation 30 format and verify them before access is granted.

faqs.q: What identification must rail safety workers carry?
faqs.a: Section 118 requires the operator to ensure each rail safety worker has identification sufficient for a rail safety officer to check the type of competence and training the worker holds for that work. The worker must produce it when a rail safety officer asks, with a maximum penalty of $2,500 for failing to do so.
